# Tool rules

Source: https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/mcp-server/tool-rules.md

Every call in the [tool reference](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/mcp-server/tools.md) follows these rules. Read them when a call is refused or reaches the wrong workspace.

## Which workspace a call reaches

**One session, one workspace.** The first call that names a working folder (`cwd`) ties the session to the workspace that holds that folder. Later calls without a `cwd` run there.

* If that folder later joins a project in another workspace, or leaves one, the session follows the folder.
* A `cwd` in another workspace is refused with `wrong_workspace` and the session's workspace name. Start a session in that workspace's folder instead.
* A folder matches its project however it is written: through a link, with `..`, or by its real path.
* Before the first `cwd`, a call goes to Personal.

Three calls cross workspaces, on purpose: `live_sessions` shows every running session on this Mac, and `recall` with `scope: "workspaces"` and `get_doc` on a shared doc read the workspaces you belong to in the cloud. An agent run's agent reaches its run by the run's token, or from inside the run's folder, wherever it lives.

## Secrets

Slate replaces keys, tokens and passwords it recognises with `[secret]` in what an agent writes through `remember`, `create_doc`, `append_to_doc`, `log_mission_progress`, `update_my_task`, and the summary of `report_agent_run_step`. It does not change `publish_artifact` and `publish_widget`, which carry code, or the `body` of `report_agent_run_step`.

## What an agent cannot do over MCP

An agent can save a typed doc and add to a doc. It cannot create a plain doc, rename, move, duplicate, move to Trash, or find and replace. Those are actions you can undo in Slate, and MCP has no undo. What an agent writes can be undone where the reverse is exact: a new doc goes to Trash, a new memory is retired.

## Find a doc by target

`get_doc` and `append_to_doc` take a **`target`** instead of an id:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `kind` | `branch` for the branch's overview, `knowledge_doc` for a typed doc under it |
| `cwd` | Your working folder. It finds the project, and its current branch when `branch` is left out |
| `branch` | The branch to look in |
| `doc_type` | The doc's type, such as `plan`, `design` or `bug-report` |
| `title` | The doc's title, when `doc_type` is not enough |

Slate writes only when the target matches exactly one doc. A target that matches more than one is refused with `ambiguous_target`.

## Home has its own tools

Home calls Slate's operations directly, not over MCP, so its tool list differs a little: it has no `slate_capabilities`, and it keeps a few finer tools of its own. See [Curated MCP commands](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/mcp-server/commands.md).

---

# Curated MCP commands

Source: https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/mcp-server/commands.md

A curated command sends a request in Home straight to one of Slate's own tools, such as creating a doc, searching memory or asking the shared workspaces, without the model choosing the tool. That is why Home works well on a small model.

## How a request runs

1. Slate matches your words to one command.
2. It fills in the arguments it already knows, such as the project and the doc type.
3. The model fills in only what is missing, such as a title.
4. Slate makes one tool call.

"Create a plan about retries" becomes `create_doc` with the type set to plan; the model writes only the title.

A command that only reads runs at once. A command that writes asks you first. Under **Auto-edit** and **Full auto** it runs without asking, except **Create an automation** and **Run an automation**, which always ask, because they spend your agent's tokens. See [Approvals](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/home/approvals.md).

## What matches

* A command that writes, such as a doc, a project, an automation or a memory, matches only when your message starts like it: "new project for…", "draft a plan…", "remember that…", after an optional "please" or "can you". "What's new in this project" is never a command.
* Anything that does not match goes to your agent, which works with its own tools.

## Your memory and your team's

**Recall what Slate remembers** searches this workspace's memory. **Ask the shared workspaces** searches what colleagues shared in every workspace you belong to, even ones this Mac has not added. "What does the team know about retries" or "has anyone solved this before" go to the shared workspaces; "what do I know about…" stays in yours. A shared answer names its author.

Naming a workspace sends the question to that workspace: "what data do I have in my Apollo workspace". The name counts only beside a word such as *workspace*, *team* or *shared*, so "fix the Apollo timeout bug" stays an ordinary request.

Your other agents reach the same two through MCP, as `recall` with `scope: "workspaces"` and `get_doc`. See the [tool reference](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/mcp-server/tools.md). **Run an automation** is `run_automation` there. **Create an automation** has no MCP tool.

See also: [Home](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/home.md), [Agents](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/agents.md).

---

# Agents

Source: https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/agents.md

An agent is an AI coding tool Slate works with. Slate runs the agent's own command-line program, under the sign-in you already have, so there is no API key to enter and no model inside Slate. Turn agents on, and pick each one's account and default model, in [Connect → Agents](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/connect.md).

## The 16 agents

The table follows the order Connect lists them. **Account folder** is the setting the agent reads to find its account, which is how Slate runs it under work or personal accounts. **Models** is the list Slate offers when it cannot ask the agent; Slate asks the agent first, so you usually see what your own account offers.

| Key | Agent | Account folder | Models |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `claude-cli` | Claude Code | `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` | `claude-sonnet-4-6` (default), `claude-opus-4-8`, `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` |
| `codex-cli` | Codex | `CODEX_HOME` | `gpt-5.3-codex` (default), `gpt-5.2` |
| `cursor-cli` | Cursor | `CURSOR_CONFIG_DIR` | What your Cursor account offers (`cursor-agent --list-models`); else `auto`, `gpt-5.3-codex`, `composer-2.5` |
| `copilot-cli` | GitHub Copilot | `COPILOT_HOME` | What your Copilot plan offers; else `gpt-4.1`, `claude-haiku-4.5`. Sign in with `copilot login` in a terminal |
| `antigravity-cli` | Antigravity | — | `auto` |
| `opencode-cli` | OpenCode | — | The providers you are logged into (`opencode models`) |
| `gemini-cli` | Gemini | `GEMINI_CLI_HOME` | `gemini-2.5-flash` (default), `gemini-2.5-pro`, `gemini-2.0-flash`. Needs a Gemini Code Assist licence or an API key |
| `cline-cli` | Cline | `CLINE_DIR` | `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5`, `anthropic/claude-opus-5.5`, `google/gemini-4-argon` |
| `grok-cli` | Grok Build | `GROK_HOME` | `grok-4.6`, `grok-4.5` |
| `kiro-cli` | Kiro | `KIRO_HOME` | `auto` |
| `qwen-cli` | Qwen Code | `QWEN_HOME` | `coder-model`, `qwen3-coder-plus`, `qwen3-coder-flash` |
| `droid-cli` | Droid | `FACTORY_HOME_OVERRIDE` | `gpt-6.1-sol` |
| `hermes-cli` | Hermes Agent | `HERMES_HOME` | `anthropic/claude-opus-4.6` |
| `goose-cli` | Goose | `GOOSE_PATH_ROOT` | `gpt-4o` |
| `kilo-cli` | Kilo Code | — | `kilo/kilo-auto/balanced`, `kilo/kilo-auto/free`, `kilo/kilo-auto/frontier` |
| `auggie-cli` | Auggie | — | `claude-sonnet-4-6` |

An agent with no account folder has one account only. Which agent can do what in Slate is in [Features by agent](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/agents/features-by-agent.md).

## Beta agents

Ten agents read **Beta** beside their name, in setup and in Connect → Agents: Antigravity, Grok Build, Kiro, Droid, Auggie, Cline, Qwen Code, Kilo Code, Hermes Agent and Goose. Slate works with them, but nobody has run a session on them yet to check every part. The label goes away when that check is done.

## Gemini needs paid access

Gemini no longer signs in personal Google accounts. It works with an API key, or with a Gemini Code Assist Standard or Enterprise licence. On a personal account it stops before it reaches Slate, so its row reads *Needs a Gemini Code Assist licence or an API key*. Antigravity is Google's agent for personal accounts.

## Which account an agent runs under

You may keep several accounts of one agent, such as work and personal Claude Code. **The workspace decides which one an agent uses**: set it in Connect → Agents. A group or a project can choose another. The same choice applies to the terminal sessions you start, and to what Slate captures. See [Project environments](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/toolkit/project-environments.md).

## Transport

Slate starts each agent's program itself, so your sign-ins never reach the app window. Claude Code and Codex speak their own protocol. The other fourteen speak the Agent Client Protocol, which lets Home stop a turn without ending the program, change the model mid-conversation and show approval cards. What differs by agent is in [Approvals](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/home/approvals.md).

## Limits on unattended runs

An automation runs with nobody watching, so Slate bounds it:

* **One $5 spend limit for the whole run.** Slate adds up the cost the agent reports. When nothing is left, the run stops and says so.
* **12 turns per run** for an agent that reports no cost.
* At most **3 agents run at once** for Home and automations together. A message waits for a free one.

Home has no step limit in Slate: the agent loops over its own tools until it is done. See [Automations](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/automations.md).

---

# Features by agent

Source: https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/agents/features-by-agent.md

The 16 agents do not all offer the same things, so this table says which agent has which feature in Slate. Every control that depends on an agent reads it: where an agent cannot do something, the control is hidden or disabled with the reason, never shown doing nothing.

Each cell is one of four answers:

- **yes**: Slate does it on this agent today.
- **not yet**: the agent can do it, and Slate does not use it yet.
- **unverified**: it may already work. Nobody has run it to check.
- **no**: the agent offers no way to do it, as measured on the date below.

## Beta agents

An agent whose **Agent driver** cell is "unverified" reads **Beta** beside its name, in setup and in Connect → Agents. Today that is ten: Antigravity, Grok Build, Kiro, Droid, Auggie, Cline, Qwen Code, Kilo Code, Hermes Agent and Goose. Slate works with them, but nobody has run a real session on them yet to check every part. An agent loses the label when its Agent driver cell turns "yes".

Gemini is not Beta, but its row reads *Needs a Gemini Code Assist licence or an API key*: Gemini no longer signs in personal Google accounts. Its "unverified" cells cannot be checked on a personal account. See [Agents](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/agents.md#gemini-needs-paid-access).

## Why some cells are "no"

Each "no" was checked against the agent's own documentation or the agent itself.

- **Budget cap and fallback model**: only Claude Code has a spend limit and fallback models. On every other agent, Slate bounds an unattended run by counting turns instead (see [Agents](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/agents.md#limits-on-unattended-runs)).
- **Background start and stop**: Codex, Gemini and OpenCode have no local way to keep a session running after you close it.
- **Cloud sessions**: Claude Code and Codex have them. Gemini, OpenCode, Cline, Qwen Code, Hermes Agent and Goose have none.
- **Structured output**: Gemini, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Droid, Auggie, Cline and Hermes Agent cannot be held to a fixed reply shape.
- **Session id known before launch**: Codex and OpenCode always choose the id themselves.
- **List running sessions**: Codex, Gemini and OpenCode list saved sessions, not running ones.
- **Name a session**: Gemini keeps no session name, so Slate keeps the one you give.
- **Multiple accounts**: OpenCode and Kilo Code have no account-folder setting, so each has one account.
- **Native memory import**: Cursor keeps its memories only in the editor's settings. OpenCode has no memory feature.
- **Save enforced at end of turn**: OpenCode, Kiro, Cline and Goose cannot hold a turn open at its end.
- **Goose has no hooks**, so Slate cannot check the save at the end of a turn or answer a tool call with an agent run's rules. Its sessions are still captured.
- **Grok Build also runs Claude Code's hooks** unless you turn that off in Grok's own settings. With both connected, Slate's hooks can run twice in one Grok session.

---

# Settings

Source: https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/settings.md

**Settings** holds what belongs to you and this computer: your account, the workspaces on this Mac, the theme, your shortcuts and the app itself. Open it from the round button near the foot of the rail. What one workspace runs, under which account, is in [Connect](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/connect.md). What Slate runs on its own is in [Automations](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/automations.md), under **Built-in**.

| Tab | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| **Account** | Who you are, and your plan |
| **Workspaces** | Every workspace on this computer: who can see it, where it lives and how big it is |
| **Appearance** | Light or dark |
| **Keyboard** | Every shortcut, and the one place to change it |
| **About** | Version, updates, logs, and what Slate may send |

## Account

* Your picture, name and email, from Google or GitHub.
* **Display name**: what people in your workspaces see on everything you publish. **Save** appears when you change it.
* **Plan**: the **Free** and **Team** cards. Team is coming; **Tell me when it's ready** records that you want it. See [Licensing and updates](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/licensing.md).
* **Sign out**.
* **Delete my account forever…**: removes your Slate account and everything you shared to a workspace. Everything on this Mac stays. You type your email to confirm. See [Privacy and security](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security.md#your-account).

## Workspaces

Lists every workspace on this computer. Click one to open its dialog, with the tabs **General**, **Members** (a shared workspace you manage) and **Storage**. **New workspace** makes one. **Sync now** pushes your work to shared workspaces and pulls your teammates' at once; it also happens every two minutes. See [Workspaces](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/workspaces.md) and [Your data and export](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/data-and-export.md).

## Appearance

Two themes, one dark and one light. Click a card to use it; the one in use says **Active**. See [Themes](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/theming.md).

## Keyboard

Every command that has a shortcut. Click a key to record a new one. See [Keyboard shortcuts](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/shortcuts.md#change-a-shortcut).

## About

* Your version, and whether an update is waiting, with **Check now** and **Install & restart**. See [Licensing and updates](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/licensing.md).
* **Website**, **Documentation** and **Source** open in your browser.
* **Logs** opens the folder of app and agent logs. Attach the latest file when you report a problem.
* **Open-source licences** lists the open-source software Slate includes.
* **Report a problem** opens the report dialog. See [Privacy and security](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security.md#reporting-a-problem).
* **Help improve Slate** holds two switches, **Anonymous usage counts** and **Crash reports**. Both are off until you turn them on. **New id** replaces the random id they are sent under.

## You, on the rail

The last button on the rail is you: your picture, or your initials when there is none. Its menu shows your name, your email, which provider you signed in with, **Account** (opens Settings → Account) and **Sign out**.

Slate downloads your picture once and keeps a copy on this Mac. Signing out removes the copy.

---

# Keyboard shortcuts

Source: https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/shortcuts.md

Every keyboard shortcut in Slate, grouped by where it works. Press **?** for a sheet of the shortcuts you can use, or open **Settings → Keyboard** to change one.

Shortcuts with ⌘ or ⌃ work while you type. A shortcut on a bare key, or on ⌥ alone, waits until you are not typing in a text field.

## Change a shortcut

**Settings → Keyboard** lists every command that has a shortcut. Click a command's key, then press the new one; Escape cancels. If another command held that key, it moves to this one and Slate says which command lost it, with **Undo**. **Unbind** removes a key, **Reset** restores one, and **Reset all** restores every key. A command has one key; there are no multi-key sequences. The palette, the **?** sheet and tooltips follow your changes at once.

The keys in the later sections (tabs and mouse, lists, the Sessions list, terminal, files) are fixed.

## Anywhere

### Navigate

| Keys | Command |
| --- | --- |
| ⌘K | **Command palette** |
| ⌘P | **Go to file or doc** |
| ⌘⇧F | **Search docs and files** |
| ⌘⇧K | **Go to Home** |
| ⌘J | **Ask AI** |
| ⌘⇧O | **Steps Ask AI ran** |
| ⌘⇧J | The session that has waited on you longest; press again for the next |
| ⌘[ and ⌘] | **Back** and **Forward** ([Back and Forward](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/search.md#back-and-forward)) |
| ⌘\` and ⌘⇧\` | **Switch to next workspace** and **Switch to previous workspace** |
| ⌃⇥ and ⌃⇧⇥ | **Next tab** and **Previous tab**, by how recently you used them |
| ⌘1 to ⌘9 | **Go to tab 1‥9**; with fewer tabs open, the last one |
| ⌘W | **Close tab**. A pinned tab stays open until you unpin it |
| ⌘⇧T | **Reopen closed tab** |
| ⌥⌘← and ⌥⌘→ | **Move tab left** and **Move tab right** |
| ⌘⇧D | **Open tab beside** the current one |
| ⇧⌘\\ | **Close split view** |

### Create

| Keys | Command |
| --- | --- |
| ⌘N | **New note** |
| ⌘⇧G | **Generate a doc** |
| ⌘⇧N | **Quick capture** |
| ⌃\` | **Open a Terminal here** |

### Doc, view and help

| Keys | Command |
| --- | --- |
| ⌘F | **Find in doc** |
| ⌘B | **Toggle sidebar** (in a doc's text, ⌘B makes bold) |
| ⌘⇧M | **Focus mode**; the same keys leave it |
| ⌘⇧L | **Toggle light / dark theme** |
| ⌘+ and ⌘− | **Increase app size** and **Decrease app size** ([Themes](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/theming.md#make-slate-bigger-or-smaller)) |
| ? | **Keyboard shortcuts** |

### In a session or a file

These are in Settings → Keyboard, and work while their panel is on screen.

| Keys | Command |
| --- | --- |
| ⌥⌘B | **Toggle session panel** |
| ⌥⌘I | **Show session details** |
| ⌥H | **Toggle file history** |
| ⌥1 and ⌥2 | **File view 1‥4**: switch a Markdown or SVG file between Preview and Read |

## Tabs and the mouse

| Gesture | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| ⌘-click a tab, a doc or a link | Open it beside the current tab |
| Double-click a tab | Keep a temporary tab open |
| Middle-click a tab | Close it |
| Drag a tab | Reorder it; pinned tabs stay at the front |
| Right-click a tab | Keep open, pin, open beside, close, close others, close to the right, close all |
| Drag the line between two columns | Resize them; double-click makes all columns equal |
| Arrow keys on that line | Resize by 16 px; with Shift, by 64 px |
| A mouse's back and forward buttons | **Back** and **Forward** |

## Lists and the palette

| Keys | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| ↑ and ↓ | Move through results |
| Enter | Open the selected row |
| Escape | Close the palette or the shortcut sheet |
| ⌘Enter | Add a line comment in a file or review, or commit from the Changes message box |
| ⌫ | Move the selected docs in the Projects tree to Trash |

## Sessions

The **Session list** keys work while focus is in the list of sessions and no text field is active.

| Key | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| ↑ / ↓ or **k** / **j** | Move between rows |
| Home and End | Jump to the first and last row |
| **f** | Start a second agent in the row's folder |
| **s** | Stop the session; press again within 4 seconds to confirm |
| Escape | Give focus back to the terminal |

## Terminal

Over a focused terminal, every ⌘ shortcut belongs to Slate except these. See [The terminal](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/sessions/terminal.md).

| Keys | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| ⌘F | Search the session, scrollback included |
| ⌘C | Copy the selection; with nothing selected, Slate's own ⌘C |
| ⌘V | Paste |
| ⌘+ / ⌘− / ⌘0 | Make the terminal font bigger, smaller, or reset it |
| ⌥⌘K | Clear |
| Shift+Enter | New line in the prompt, without sending |
| ⌥← / ⌥→ / ⌥⌫ | Jump a word left or right; remove a word |
| Ctrl-C | In an agent's session: asks whether to end it. In a Terminal: sent to the program |

## Files and the editor

| Keys | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| ⌘S | Save |
| ⌘F | Find and replace |
| [ and ] | Step through changes (not while typing) |
| Escape | Leave Diff or a past commit |
| ⌘Z / ⌘⇧Z | Undo and redo |
| ⌥-click | Add a cursor |
| ⌥⇧-drag | Select a column |
| ⌘D | Select the next match |
| ⌘⇧L | Select every match |
| Ctrl+G | Go to line |
| ⌘/ | Comment |
| ⌥↑ / ⌥↓ | Move a line |
| ⇧⌥↑ / ⇧⌥↓ | Copy a line |
| ⇧⌘K | Remove a line |
| Enter or Tab | Take an offered word |

See [Files, memories and editing](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/sessions/files.md).

## Home and Ask AI

In the box on Home and in the ⌘J panel, **⇧⇥** moves the mode one step: **Ask first**, **Auto-edit**, **Full auto**, then **Ask first** again. On Home, the arrow keys turn the deck of cards.

# Privacy and security

Source: https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security.md

**Sign in once. Your work never leaves your Mac** without an action you take. Your workspaces are files on your Mac: `workspace.db` for Personal, one file for each shared workspace, and `machine.db` for what describes this computer. Below is every case where data leaves, and how to turn each one off. The legal text is the [Privacy policy](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/legal/privacy-policy.md).

More detail: [Where each piece of data lives](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security/where-data-lives.md), [Workspace sharing, precisely](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security/sharing.md), [Security details](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security/security-details.md).

## Your account

You sign in with Google or GitHub. The account holds your name, email and picture link, which provider you used, and your plan. If you pressed **Tell me when it's ready** for Team, it also records that you asked, and from which screen. It holds none of your docs, sessions or memories.

The sign-in is kept in a file on your Mac that only you can read, so later launches work offline. When you are online, Slate contacts its cloud at each start and whenever the sign-in renews. Those requests carry your account id and your IP address, and no workspace content. The sign-in service also keeps logs with your IP address.

Slate downloads your picture once from Google or GitHub and keeps a copy on your Mac. Signing out removes the copy.

**Delete your account forever.** **Settings → Account → Delete my account forever…** removes your account from Slate's cloud: your name, email, plan, Team interest, your memberships and the content of everything you shared to a workspace. Your teammates' Macs remove their copies on the next sync. You are signed out, and everything on this Mac stays. If other people are in your account or its workspaces, Slate asks you to remove them first.

## What leaves your Mac

Four exceptions run without a click each time. Three of them need your choice first. The update check is on by default, and you can turn it off.

| Exception | What leaves | When, and how to stop it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Your agents** | Your prompt and context, sent by the agent's own program to its own provider, under its own sign-in. A [cloud session](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/sessions/cloud.md) also sends the project's code. **On my phone** connects a session to claude.ai | When you use Home, a session, an agent run or an automation, or on a schedule you set |
| **A shared workspace** | Everything in a workspace you share or join, except what [sharing](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security/sharing.md) lists as never sent | Only after you share a workspace or join one. Sharing needs the Team plan |
| **The update check** | Your app version, system, chip, whether you run a prerelease, and a random install id. No workspace content | 8 seconds after the window opens, then every 4 hours, and on **Check now** in Settings → About. Turn it off with **Automatic updates** in [Automations](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/automations/built-in.md) |
| **Telemetry** | **Anonymous usage counts**: three events (Slate opened, a session captured, a memory recalled), with the agent's name. **Crash reports**: the error's type and where in Slate's code it happened, never its text | Only after you turn it on in **Settings → About**. Both are off by default |

The install id is 16 random bytes made on your Mac. It says nothing about you or your Mac, and it is not the telemetry id. It places your copy in a stable group when a new version goes out to part of the installed copies first. Slate's update service keeps no record of it, but it appears in the short-lived request logs of the service's host. Remove the `install-id` file from Slate's data folder and Slate makes a new one.

The telemetry id and both switches belong to this computer, not to a workspace. **New id** replaces the id.

Slate ships no model and downloads none. Memory search runs on your Mac.

## Requests and connections you start

* **Git.** When you press the button for it, git and `gh` fetch, pull, push and open pull requests against your own remote.
* **Integrations.** An app you connect is read with the sign-in you gave it, sent only to that app's address. GitHub is read through your own `gh` sign-in. **Disconnect** stops it.
* **Widgets.** A widget's GitHub action (approve, request changes, comment, label) runs only after you confirm the card that names the account.
* **Live artifacts.** A live artifact can load a script from cdnjs, jsDelivr or unpkg, and that host sees the address it asks for.

None of these sends a doc, a session or a memory of yours.

## Reporting a problem

A report leaves only when you press **Send report**. Open the dialog from **Report this** on an error, from **Report a problem** in ⌘K, or from **Report…** in Settings → About. The dialog shows everything that is sent before you send it:

* what you wrote;
* which screen you were on (this can name a project and a branch), and the error's text if you reported from an error;
* your Slate version, macOS version and chip;
* the last 40 lines of the app log, unless you untick them.

Every file path is shown as `~/…` before you see it. Nothing else is cleaned, so read the lines, and untick the log if it holds something you would not send. A report carries no doc, session or conversation content, no account details and no install id. It goes to Slate's cloud, where only the Slate team can read it. What you wrote, the screen, the error and the version are copied to a private GitHub issue so the team can track the fix.

## How long the cloud keeps it

| What | How long |
| --- | --- |
| Usage counts and crash reports | 180 days |
| Problem reports | 12 months. The GitHub issue copy is removed on request |
| Your account, profile, plan, Team interest and sign-in logs | Until you delete your account forever |
| Invitations | Until they are accepted or declined |
| Shared workspace rows you wrote | Until you withdraw them, stop sharing, use **Erase my work**, or delete your account forever |
| Request logs of the update service and the release host | A short time, set by those hosts |

To have usage counts already sent removed, email your telemetry id to the address below before you press **New id**.

## Reporting a vulnerability

Email **slate.ai.app@gmail.com** with a description, the steps to reproduce it and what an attacker gains. Expect a reply within 72 hours, and a fix within 7 days for anything critical. Good-faith research is welcome: stay within what shows the issue, do not degrade the app for others, and allow time before you disclose it.

---

# Where each piece of data lives

Source: https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security/where-data-lives.md

Everything Slate keeps is on your Mac, in Slate's data folder: `~/Library/Application Support/app.slate.workspace/`. No server holds your workspace. A shared workspace sends only what [sharing](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security/sharing.md) lists.

## Your data

| What | Where | Shared? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Personal workspace | `workspace.db`. You can move it: see [Your data and export](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/data-and-export.md) | Only if you share Personal |
| Each shared workspace | Its own file in the data folder | Yes, see [sharing](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security/sharing.md) |
| Docs, memories, sessions, automations | Inside their workspace's file | With their workspace, except what sharing withholds |
| Images in docs | Files beside the database, in the `files` folder | With a shared doc that names them |
| This computer's settings, the telemetry id and switches, and the list of workspaces on this Mac | `machine.db` | Never |
| Token use per session ([Activity](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/activity.md)): times, token counts, model, cost. Never prompt or reply text | `machine.db` | Never |
| Tasks from your integrations: one line each, never a description, comment or message text | The workspace's file | Never |
| An agent run's drafts (pull request text, ticket update, review comments), so you can read them before you approve | The workspace's file, removed 30 days after the run closes | Never |
| Receipts: per session, the last reply's first paragraph, commands with their result counts, edited files and commits | The workspace's file | Never |
| Slate's own cost: CPU, memory and wake counts every 15 minutes | `slate.log` in `~/Library/Logs/app.slate.workspace/` | Never sent |
| Your agents' sign-ins | Not in Slate. Each agent keeps its own | Never |

## Credential files

Slate keeps these files in its data folder, readable only by your user. None of them is inside a database, so exporting a workspace never hands anyone a live credential. They stay in the data folder when you move Personal.

| File | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `cloud-session.json` | Your Slate sign-in |
| `slate-server-token` | The key every local caller presents to Slate's local server. Kept across launches. No agent's setup holds it ([how](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security/security-details.md#the-local-server)) |
| `slate-mcp-token` | A second key that opens only Slate's MCP server. Slate gives it to the sessions it starts; no agent's config file holds it |
| `work-gateway-auth.json` | The token an integration you connected from Slate issued to Slate. Sent only to that server |
| `work-token-auth.json` | A token you pasted for an integration. Sent only to that server, never logged, removed on **Disconnect** |
| `oauth-pending.json` | A sign-in to an integration still in progress. Removed when used, or after 15 minutes |

Back to [Privacy and security](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security.md).

---

# Workspace sharing, precisely

Source: https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security/sharing.md

Nothing is shared until you share a workspace or join one. Then the rows you write in it are copied to Slate's cloud, where its members can read them. Here is what goes, what never goes, and how to take it back.

* A workspace you never shared has no copy in the cloud, so nothing about it is sent.
* **Personal** starts unshared. Before you share it, Slate shows how much it would publish. It holds more than you wrote there: memories saved outside every project (a session in a folder no project holds is not recorded, but a memory it saves is global).
* While no workspace is shared, Slate makes no sync requests.

## What a shared workspace sends

| What | What is sent |
| --- | --- |
| Docs | Title, content, a plain-text copy for search, the doc type, the parent link and the doc's branch label |
| Memories | The sentence, its kind, subject and confidence, a lesson's trigger, and the title of the doc it was learned on |
| Development activity | Commits (the subject line only), branch events, and a record that an AI session happened, with its branch and time |
| Artifacts | Title, kind, description, the agent that made it, the doc it was made under, and its newest version |
| Doc images | The images a shared doc names, in private storage only the workspace's members can read |
| You | Your display name, email and picture from Google or GitHub |

## What is never sent

From any workspace, shared or not:

* a project's or group's folder path, and the other details Slate keeps about a doc;
* the folder path of a commit (the git remote address is sent instead), its message beyond the subject line, its counts of files and lines, and lists of the files you touched;
* the text of an AI session, and the doc a captured session is kept in;
* the reasoning behind a memory;
* a memory that belongs to no doc, a memory you hid from sessions, and a memory a widget saved;
* your settings.

> **Warning:** **Text is sent as written.** A doc's content and a memory's sentence are not filtered. If you typed a folder path into a doc, it goes with the doc. Slate does replace keys, tokens and passwords it recognises with `[secret]` in every memory, and in docs an agent writes. A doc you type yourself is not checked, and neither is an artifact or a widget.

## Who can read and write

* **Each doc has one writer, its author.** Members read your docs and can never change them.
* **The cloud decides who sees what.** A person who is not a member of a workspace cannot read its rows.
* **Your Mac keeps your teammates' names.** To show who wrote what while offline, Slate keeps the name, email and picture of each member of your shared workspaces in `machine.db`. Leaving a workspace removes them.

## Take back what you shared

* **Stop sharing**: the **Sharing** switch in **Settings → Workspaces**, in the workspace's **General** tab. It shows a count first. Slate stops publishing and blanks what you published; every member's copy drops it on their next sync. Your own copy stays. Sharing again publishes it again.
* **Move a doc out**: it is withdrawn on the next sync.
* **Erase my work**: removes every row you wrote in that workspace, for every member, while you stay in it. Sharing again does not bring them back. Editors and owners can do this.

> **Warning:** Withdrawing removes your rows from the cloud. It cannot remove what members already read. Images are not withdrawn yet: they stay in the workspace's private storage, readable only by its members.

## Widgets and live artifacts

**A live artifact** can read docs, memories and sessions of its own project, read-only. It cannot connect to any address, except to load a script from cdnjs, jsDelivr or unpkg; that host sees the address it asks for. See [Artifacts](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/artifacts.md).

**A widget** has no network at all. It reads what its tab shows. A write needs a permission you granted once, and a memory or doc write shows its words every time before it saves. Three permissions reach further:

| Permission | What it allows | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub read | Read-only GitHub requests with your own `gh` sign-in. The widget never sees the token | 12 a minute |
| MCP read | A tool you allowed for that widget, read-only, from a server of the widget's own workspace | 20 a minute per server |
| GitHub act | Ask to approve, request changes on, comment on or label a pull request, with words you type. A card names the account every time | 5 an hour per widget, 20 an hour for all widgets |

A teammate's widget or live artifact never reads your workspace. See [Widgets](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/widgets.md).

---

# Security details

Source: https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security/security-details.md

This guide is for anyone who checks Slate's security: what guards the local server, what Slate writes into other programs, what it does not encrypt, and how to manage it on company Macs. To report a vulnerability, see [Privacy and security](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security.md#reporting-a-vulnerability).

## Your agents' setup files

* **No API keys.** Your agents make their own model calls under their own sign-in. Slate stores no provider key.
* **Nothing is written until you connect an agent.** You connect one in setup or in [Connect → Agents](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/connect.md). From then on Slate keeps the agents you install later connected too. Turning that off removes what Slate wrote, and it stays off.
* **Slate keeps a copy before it changes a file.** It keeps the five newest copies of each file it rewrote. Copies you made yourself are never touched.

## The local server

Slate's local server listens only on your own computer (loopback).

* **It answers only Slate.** It refuses a request that comes from any web page other than Slate's own window, and a request addressed to any host name other than this computer.
* **Every caller shows a key.** The key is in `slate-server-token`, a file only your user can read. The key is kept across launches. Another program can call the server only by reading that file.
* **Agents get a narrower key.** The sessions Slate starts reach its MCP server with a second key, `slate-mcp-token`, which opens the MCP tools and nothing else.
* **Tool arguments are checked.** Every MCP call's arguments are checked against the tool's rules first. A wrong argument is refused, never guessed.

## Sign-in

Your Slate sign-in opens your system browser and comes back to Slate's local server, which finishes it. No code, token or password passes through the app window. The sign-in is kept in a file only your user can read, never in a database.

## Workspaces stay apart

Each workspace stays in its own file, and Slate does not mix them.

* A session works in the workspace of the first folder it names. A folder from another workspace is refused.
* A file records which workspace it is, so a file in the wrong place does not open as another workspace.
* Three things cross workspaces, on purpose: Sessions and the `live_sessions` tool show every running session on this Mac; `recall` with `scope: "workspaces"` and `get_doc` on a shared doc read the workspaces you belong to in the cloud.

## What Slate does not encrypt

**Slate encrypts nothing at rest.** Your workspace files, `machine.db` and the sign-in files are not encrypted by Slate. Their safety rests on FileVault and on file permissions. Anyone who can read your user's files can read every workspace. If you need encryption inside the app, Slate does not offer it today.

The app window runs under a content security policy, so it cannot reach arbitrary addresses on the network.

## Backups and restore

* Every change is saved as one complete step, so a crash never leaves half a change.
* Before an update changes a workspace's format, Slate copies the workspace aside and keeps the last three copies.
* **Settings → Workspaces**, the workspace, **Storage**, **Restore a backup** lists them. A restore runs at the next start, and the workspace it replaces is kept as a backup too. If a connected agent still has the workspace open, the restore does not run; quit the agent and try again.

See [Your data and export](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/data-and-export.md).

## Managed Macs

For IT teams that deploy Slate with an MDM such as Jamf, Kandji or Intune.

* **Start at login is a managed setting.** Push a configuration profile for the domain `app.slate.workspace` with the key `StartAtLogin`, true or false. Slate then follows it on every Mac, and the switch in **Automations › Built-in** reads **Managed by your organization** and cannot be changed.
* **The login item** is registered by the signed app from inside its bundle, under the label `app.slate.workspace.login`. Slate writes nothing to `~/Library/LaunchAgents`. A Login Items profile (`com.apple.servicemanagement`) can allow it with a `Label` rule for `app.slate.workspace.login`, or a `BundleIdentifier` rule for `app.slate.workspace`. Slate is signed with its own certificate, not an Apple Developer ID, so there is no team identifier to match.
* **What runs at login**: the app with no window, its menu bar icon and its local server, so agents can reach Slate. A signed-out Slate opens its window to ask for sign-in.

---

# Your data and export

Source: https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/data-and-export.md

Each workspace is one SQLite file on your Mac, and it holds everything in that workspace: docs, sessions, memories, automations and settings. You can copy it, move it, back it up and open it with any SQLite tool. There is no copy in the cloud unless you share the workspace. See [Workspace sharing, precisely](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security/sharing.md).

## Find the file

Personal is at `~/Library/Application Support/app.slate.workspace/workspace.db`. Each shared workspace has its own file in the same folder.

Everything below is in **Settings → Workspaces**: click the workspace, then the **Storage** tab. It shows where the file is, with **Open** to show it in Finder, and how big it is.

## Export

**Export** saves a copy of the workspace's file anywhere you choose. It works while Slate is open, and for a workspace that has gone read-only. The copy is the same SQLite file, with no conversion.

## Move Personal to another folder

**Move…** moves Personal to another folder or an external drive. Slate restarts to finish the move. It copies the file, checks the copy, and only then uses it. The old file stays where it was, as a backup; move it to the Trash yourself once everything has arrived. Your agents and Slate's backups follow the move.

Only Personal can move. A shared workspace stays in Slate's data folder. Slate refuses a folder that iCloud Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive or Google Drive syncs, and a network drive: the database cannot run safely there.

If the folder is not there when Slate starts, for example a drive that is not plugged in, Slate shows *Slate cannot find your workspace* and opens nothing in its place. You can choose another location, or **Start empty here**. When the moved workspace is back, **Use a workspace from another folder…** in Storage points Slate at it. **Go back to the default location** returns Personal to the data folder.

## Shrink the file

The **Storage** tab shows the file's size and how much of it is space left by removed items. SQLite does not give that space back by itself. **Reclaim** returns it to the disk now; Slate also does it at launch when enough is worth returning.

## Restore a backup

Before an update changes a workspace's format, Slate copies it aside and keeps the last three copies. **Restore a backup** in Storage lists them. The restore runs when Slate next starts, and the workspace it replaces is kept as a backup too, so it can be undone. Quit every agent connected to Slate first: if one still has the workspace open, the restore does not run.

To go back to an older version of Slate, restore the backup taken before the upgrade, then install the older version. An older Slate refuses to open a workspace a newer one has changed.

## Delete a workspace forever

**Delete workspace forever**, in the workspace's **General** tab, removes the file and its backups. Nothing is kept. Export first if you may want it back. Personal cannot be removed.

## What an export leaves out

* **Your sign-in.** It is in its own file, never in a database, so an export cannot hand anyone a live credential.
* **Images in docs.** They are files beside the database, in the `files` folder of Slate's data folder. Copy that folder with the export to keep them.

And what an export carries that you may not expect:

* **A shared workspace's export holds your teammates' work too**, as your copy has synced it.
* **A project's memory settings** are inside the file.

## Read the file yourself

The file is standard SQLite, so you can read it years from now with other tools. The main tables are `doc` (docs and projects), `memory`, `routine` (automations), `task` (your Tasks list), `agent_run`, `artifact`, `activity` and `setting`. Doc content is stored as JSON blocks.

---

# Licensing and updates

Source: https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/licensing.md

Slate is free for individuals. The **Free** plan is everything Slate does on this Mac, with no card, no time limit and no licence key. **Team** is for sharing a workspace with your team. It is coming and has no price yet.

## Your plan

**Settings → Account** shows your plan as two cards, **Free** and **Team**. Press **Tell me when it's ready** on the Team card and Slate emails you when Team is ready; the button then reads **We'll email you**. An account with early access to Team reads **Early access** and can share workspaces now.

Slate is proprietary software, licensed under the [Terms of use](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/legal/terms-of-use.md). Your workspace stays yours on every plan: it is a file on your Mac that you can always open and export.

## Updates

Slate checks for a new version 8 seconds after it opens, then every 4 hours while it stays open. A Slate started at login with no window checks after about 10 minutes, then about every 4 hours. What a check sends is in [Privacy and security](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security.md#what-leaves-your-mac).

When a new version exists, Slate downloads it in the background and tells you it is ready. On a Mac it usually downloads only what changed since your version. It installs only if the result is exactly the published release and its signature checks out; otherwise it downloads the whole version.

The update installs **when you next quit**. Slate never restarts itself while you work. To install sooner, press **Restart now**; if Slate hosts sessions, it first says how many a restart ends.

New versions can go out to part of the installed copies first. A version that is stopped after it downloaded is not installed.

**Settings → About** shows your version, a waiting update with its release notes, and **Check now**. A failed check or install says why, with **Try again**.

To stop the automatic check and download, turn off **Automatic updates** in **Automations › Built-in**. **Check now** still works, and a downloaded update waits for **Restart now**.

## If Slate will not start

After three launches in a row fail to finish starting, the next one opens in **safe mode**: *Slate started in safe mode*. It skips the watcher, background automations and everything else that is not needed to fix it, and checks for an update at once. Your workspace file is not touched.

* **Start normally** tries a normal launch again.
* **Open logs** shows the log folder, for a problem report.

## See also

* [Platform and availability](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/platform.md)
* [Privacy and security](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security.md)

# Platform and availability

Source: https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/platform.md

Slate is a native app for macOS 13.5 (Ventura) or later. There is one app for Apple Silicon and one for Intel, and the installer picks the one for your Mac. An older macOS refuses to open the app.

**Linux and Windows are paused.** New releases are for macOS only. Earlier releases that included a Linux `.deb` or a Windows installer stay available on GitHub, but they no longer get updates.

## Platform support today

| Platform | Can you download it? | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| macOS, Apple Silicon | **Yes** — the `curl` installer | Primary platform, smoke-tested |
| macOS, Intel | **Yes** — the `curl` installer | Its own app, built on the release Mac for Intel. Before each release it boots, and its sidecar builds an app, through Rosetta |

## Install

Run the `curl` command in [Install and first ten minutes](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/overview/getting-started.md#install). It downloads the app, checks its checksum and Slate's own signature, and installs it to `/Applications`. There is no Homebrew cask and no App Store listing.

Each release also has a `.dmg` for each chip. It is not the supported way to install. Slate is signed with its own certificate and is not notarized by Apple, so macOS blocks a disk image a browser downloaded, with *Apple could not verify Slate is free of malware*. On macOS 15 and later, only **System Settings → Privacy & Security** lets it open. The `curl` installer avoids this.

## Remove

Run the command in [Uninstalling](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/overview/uninstalling.md). It takes Slate out of your agents, removes the app and keeps your workspace unless you ask otherwise.

## See also

* [Licensing and updates](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/licensing.md)
* [What Slate costs your machine](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/footprint.md)

---

# What Slate costs your machine

Source: https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/footprint.md

**When nothing changes, Slate does nothing.** If you are not typing, no file changed and no AI session is writing, Slate uses almost no CPU and wakes your Mac as little as it can. The numbers below are the most Slate may use. Slate's tests measure every change against them, and a change that goes over a limit fails. Limits only go down.

"% of one core" is the share of one processor core: 100% is one core fully busy, and your Mac has several.

<!-- footprint:begin — written by scripts/gate/footprint-doc.mjs from scripts/gate/footprint-budget.json. Edit the budget, then run it. -->
### With the window open and idle

| Screen open | At most, % of one core |
| --- | --- |
| Sessions | 1.5% |
| Home | 0.4% |
| Projects | 1.5% |
| Tasks | 0.6% |
| Memory | 1% |
| Activity | 0.6% |
| Artifacts | 4.5% |
| Widgets | 3.5% |
| Automations | 1.5% |
| Toolkit | 0.4% |
| Connect | 2% |
| Trash | 0.6% |
| Settings | 1.5% |
| Window hidden | 3% |

### Started at login, no window

When Slate starts at login, it loads no window until you open it: only the app, its menu bar icon and the server run. Together they use at most 0.2% of one core and 278 MB of memory, with no webview loaded.

### Slate's server, idle

| Store | CPU, % of one core | Wake-ups per second | Memory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A new user | 0.05% | 0.2 | 138 MB |
| Six months of use | 0.05% | 0.2 | 208 MB |
| A heavy user | 0.05% | 0.2 | 236 MB |

In use, on the heavy store with an agent's sessions captured and Tasks, Sessions and Memory opened, the memory the server's code still uses two minutes after launch is at most 51 MB. It counts what the code keeps, not what macOS has not taken back yet, so it is smaller than the table above.

With a window open and nothing running, the server wakes at most 0.3 times per second.

### Slate's server, while AI sessions work

Two sessions working, one of them writing every 2 seconds, on the six-months store.

| What | At most |
| --- | --- |
| CPU, % of one core | 2% |
| Programs it starts on its own, per second | 0 |
| Times it re-asks an agent about a session in a long tool call, per second | 0.05 |

### Download and disk

Each kind of Mac has its own download, since 0.1.55:

| Chip | Download (.dmg), at most | Installed app (.app), at most |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Apple Silicon | 132 MB | 403 MB |
| Intel | 132 MB | 403 MB |

Measured on a MacBook Pro with an Apple M4 Pro (14 cores, 48 GB of memory) on macOS 26. MB is 1,024 × 1,024 bytes.
<!-- footprint:end -->

The tests use no data of yours. They build their own stores (a new user, six months of use, a heavy user) and launch their own copy of the app. A number over its limit is measured again, and counts only if both runs are over. The limits come from the Mac named under the tables; a slower Mac may show a higher percentage for the same idle Slate.

## Check it yourself

Use Activity Monitor (Applications → Utilities).

1. Leave Slate open on any screen and do not touch it for a minute.
2. In the **CPU** tab, search for `Slate`. You see the app and its server (`slate-mcp`). Add their **% CPU**. The limits also count the web view's helper processes, so the real total is a little higher.
3. In the **Energy** tab, read Slate's **Energy Impact** and **Avg Energy Impact**. An idle Slate sits near zero. A high average while you did not use it is worth reporting.
4. Hide the window (⌘H) and look again. That is the "Window hidden" row.

Your numbers can be higher than the idle limits for a good reason. While an AI session writes, Slate reads it as it happens; the "while AI sessions work" limit covers that. Slate starts no programs on a timer to check on a session.

* [Platform and availability](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/platform.md)
* [Privacy and security](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/privacy-and-security.md)

# Privacy policy

<!-- Factual update 2026-11-08. Still a template: counsel must review before release. -->

# Privacy Policy

## Contents

- [Your Account](#your-account)
- [What Slate Stores, and Where](#what-slate-stores-and-where)
- [What Leaves Your Device, and When](#what-leaves-your-device-and-when)
- [How Long the Cloud Keeps It](#how-long-the-cloud-keeps-it)
- [No Tracking, No Sale of Data](#no-tracking-no-sale-of-data)
- [Third-Party Model Providers](#third-party-model-providers)
- [Service Providers](#service-providers)
- [Your Control, Export, and Deletion](#your-control-export-and-deletion)
- [Children](#children)
- [Changes to This Policy](#changes-to-this-policy)
- [Contact](#contact)
- [See also](#see-also)

> **Note:** This is a template/placeholder legal document for a product still in development.
> It is not legal advice and does not create a contract. It should be reviewed and
> completed by qualified counsel before any commercial release, and jurisdiction,
> contact, and licensing details filled in.

Slate is a local-first desktop application. It is built so that your workspace lives
on your machine and nothing leaves it without an explicit action on your part. This
policy explains what Slate stores, where it stores it, and the narrow set of cases
where data crosses the boundary of your device.

The short version: you sign in once with Google or GitHub, your account holds your name,
email and plan, your workspace is a file you own, and the only workspace content that
ever reaches a server is what is in a workspace you specifically choose to share.

## Your Account

Slate requires an account. On first launch you sign in with Google or GitHub. Sign-in is
handled by Supabase Auth, in Slate's own Supabase project. The account holds:

- your name, email address and picture link, as supplied by Google or GitHub;
- which of the two providers you signed in with;
- your plan (Free, or Team when it is available);
- if you asked to hear when Team is ready, that you asked and from which screen.

The account holds none of your docs, sessions or memories. The sign-in session is kept
in a permission-restricted file (`cloud-session.json`) in Slate's application-data folder,
never inside a database, so later launches work offline.

When you are online, Slate contacts its Supabase project at each start and whenever the
sign-in token renews. It renews the token, makes sure your account exists, and reads which
workspaces you belong to. Those requests carry your account id and your IP address, and no
workspace content. Supabase Auth also keeps sign-in logs that hold your IP address.

**Your picture.** When your account has a picture, Slate downloads it once from your
provider's picture host (`avatars.githubusercontent.com` for GitHub, `googleusercontent.com`
for Google) and keeps a copy in the `account-photo` folder in Slate's application-data folder.
It downloads again only when the picture link changes. Like any web request, this reveals
your IP address to that provider. Signing out deletes the copy. Without a picture, or
offline, Slate shows your initials.

**Invitations.** When you invite someone to a shared workspace, their email address and the
role you chose are stored in our database until they accept or decline. Slate sends no
email: the invitation opens in your own mail app, and you send it.

## What Slate Stores, and Where

Everything you create in Slate — docs, the block-editor content, agent runs, captured
AI sessions, decisions, memories, automations, skills, and settings — is stored
locally in SQLite database files on your device: `workspace.db` for your Personal
workspace, one more file for each shared workspace, and `machine.db` for the settings
that describe this computer.

Slate stores no embeddings and downloads no machine-learning model. Memory is retrieved
by keyword matching computed on your device, re-ordered by word statistics that Slate
fits in memory from your own stored memories and never writes to disk or sends anywhere.

| Item | Location |
|---|---|
| Workspace database | See per-platform paths below |
| Sign-in session | A permission-restricted file (`cloud-session.json`) in Slate's application-data folder, never inside a database |
| Your picture | A copy in the `account-photo` folder in Slate's application-data folder, deleted when you sign out |

The workspace database lives at:

```
macOS    ~/Library/Application Support/app.slate.workspace/workspace.db
Linux    $XDG_DATA_HOME/app.slate.workspace/
Windows  %APPDATA%\app.slate.workspace\
```

You can override the location with the `SLATE_DB_PATH` environment variable. The
database uses WAL mode, and Slate takes an automatic backup before running schema
migrations.

Slate holds no provider API keys. Where Slate drives a command-line tool (see below),
that tool holds its own authentication under its own configuration. Your Slate sign-in
session token is written to a permission-restricted
file in Slate's application-data folder rather than inside any database, so exporting your
workspace cannot hand anyone a live credential.

## What Leaves Your Device, and When

Slate's default posture is that nothing leaves the machine. Apart from your sign-in
(above), four standing exceptions run without a click each time. Three of them need your
choice or your opt-in first. The update check runs by default, and you can switch it off.
A problem report you send, requests you start yourself and connections you set up are
described after the four.

1. **Model calls made by your own installed CLIs.** Slate's model providers (called
   "agents") drive command-line tools you have already installed and authenticated —
   the agents you connect (16 supported, see the [docs](https://liozelmalem-star.github.io/slate-releases/docs/features/agents.md)). When you use Home, a
   session, an agent run or an automation, the relevant CLI sends your prompt and context
   to that provider to generate a response, when you ask it to or on a schedule you set.
   A cloud session sends your project's code to the vendor's computer (Claude Code clones
   the project's GitHub remote, or uploads the code if there is none). **On my phone**
   connects a session to claude.ai, and Anthropic keeps that conversation. Slate does not hold a raw provider API key; the CLI makes the request
   under its own account and its own terms. What is sent, and to whom, is governed by
   the provider you chose (see "Third-Party Model Providers" below).

2. **The contents of a shared workspace you create or join.** Slate includes an optional
   team layer. Sharing a workspace needs the Team plan. Every workspace is unshared until you
   choose to share it, and a workspace that has never been shared has no counterpart in our
   database at all — nothing about it is transmitted, and nothing can be.
   Your **Personal** workspace begins unshared. Choosing to share it shows you a count of
   what would be published before you confirm.

   Within a shared workspace, the rows you author are copied to a hosted Postgres database
   (Supabase) where that workspace's members can read them. What is sent is:

   - **Docs** — title, block content, a plain-text rendering of that content for search,
     the document type, and the parent link.
   - **Memories** — the saved sentence, its kind, its subject, its confidence, for a
     lesson the trigger that says when it applies, and the title of the doc it was
     learned against.
   - **Development activity** — commits (the subject line only, never the rest of the commit
     message), branch created / deleted / merged / switched events, and
     a record that an AI session happened (its branch and the time).
   - **Artifacts** — the docs an agent publishes to be looked at: the title, the kind
     (an HTML page or slides), the description, the name of the agent that made it, the doc it
     was made under, and the content of its newest version.
   - **Doc images** — the image files a shared doc names. Each goes to a private storage
     bucket that only the workspace's members can read; the doc row carries only its address.
   - **Your identity** — the display name, email address, and avatar supplied by your
     sign-in provider.

   What is **never** sent, from any workspace: your doc metadata (the `properties` bag,
   which is where a project's or a group's folder path is held), except a doc's git branch
   label, which is a branch name and not a path, the absolute path recorded against a
   commit (the normalised git remote URL is sent in its place), counts of files and lines
   changed, per-file lists of the files you touched or staged, the contents of any AI session
   transcript and the doc a captured AI session is stored as, the reasoning text behind
   a memory, any memory that belongs to no doc, any memory you hid from sessions, any memory
   an app saved, and your application settings. The set of activity types that may be stored
   is enforced by a constraint in the database itself, not only by the application.

   **What we cannot filter is the text itself.** A doc's body and a memory's sentence
   are sent as written. If you typed a filesystem path into a doc, or an agent recorded one
   inside a decision it wrote, that text is transmitted with the rest of the row. Slate replaces
   recognised secrets (tokens in a published key format, and assignments that name themselves
   a secret) with `[secret]` in memories, in docs an agent writes and in task reports; it does
   not otherwise inspect or redact prose. The structured places a path is held are withheld; a path
   written in a sentence is content, and content in a shared workspace is what a shared
   workspace is for.

   Sharing is one-way. Other members can read what you wrote but cannot modify it, and
   nothing another member writes is ever copied over a doc of yours. Moving a doc out of a
   shared workspace withdraws it on the next synchronisation, and **Erase my work** removes
   every row you authored in that workspace for every member — though, as with any
   publication, withdrawal is not retroactive. Access is enforced by database-level row
   security, so a person who is not a member of a workspace cannot read its contents.

3. **The update check.** Slate asks its update service, and the release host if the service
   does not answer, whether a newer version exists. No workspace content is sent. The
   request carries your app version, your operating system and
   processor type, whether you run a prerelease, and a random **install id**. The install
   id is 16 random bytes generated on your machine the first time Slate starts, kept in
   the file `install-id` in Slate's data folder. It is not derived from your hardware, your
   hostname, your account or anything else about you, and it is not the telemetry id
   below. Its only use is to place your copy in a stable group when a new version is
   offered to part of the installed copies first. The update service stores no record of
   it, but the id is part of the request, so it appears, with your IP address, in the request
   logs that the service's host (Supabase) keeps for a short time. Deleting the file makes Slate generate a new id. Before it installs a downloaded
   update, Slate asks the service whether that version was withdrawn, sending only the
   version number. Like any web request, these reveal your IP address and that you run
   Slate. It runs eight seconds after the window opens and every four hours while it stays open,
   about ten minutes after a Slate started at login without a window and then about every four hours, and
   whenever you press "Check now" in Settings → About. When a newer version exists, Slate
   also downloads it from the release host, GitHub Releases, in the background, and installs it when you next
   quit. You can switch the automatic check and download off in Automations › Built-in
   (Automatic updates); the manual check still works.

4. **Opt-in telemetry.** Slate can report anonymous usage counts and crash reports.
   Both are **off** until you turn them on, in Settings → About, and they are separate
   switches. What is sent is a closed list, enforced in code rather than promised here:

   - **Usage counts** — three events only: Slate was opened, a session was captured, a
     memory was recalled. Each carries a random installation id, the app version,
     the operating system name, the time, and, for a captured session or a recall, which AI
     tool it was: one of the 16 agents Slate supports, or other. Nothing else.
   - **Crash reports** — the *type* of error (for example `TypeError`) and where in
     Slate's own code it happened. The error's own text is never sent: it is written
     wherever the failure occurred, so it can quote whatever Slate was working on at the
     time, and no rule about future code could keep that safe. Only the type and the call
     stack travel, and the stack is reduced to its call lines, at most twenty. Each keeps
     its function name, file name and line number. Directories are stripped, and every line
     that is not a call line is dropped, the one that would have carried the message
     included.

   The installation id is 16 random bytes generated on your machine. It is not derived
   from your hardware, your hostname, your account, or anything else about you, and you
   can replace it at any time with the "New id" button beside it. To have counts already
   sent deleted, email that id to the contact below before you press "New id"; otherwise
   they are deleted after 180 days.

   **The id and both consent switches are per machine, not per workspace** — they live
   in `machine.db`, the same file that holds your other app-level settings, never inside
   `workspace.db`. Deleting a workspace database does not touch them: turning both
   switches off, or pressing "New id", is how you reset telemetry. Deleting `machine.db`
   itself removes the id and both switches along with every other machine-level setting.

   No doc content, no session content, no conversation content, and no file paths are
   ever included in either channel.

**A problem report you send.** When you press **Send report** in the report dialog, Slate
sends what you wrote, which screen you were on (which can name a project and a branch), the
text of the error you reported from (if any), your Slate version, your macOS version and
your chip, and, unless you untick it, the last 40 lines of the app log. Every file path in
the error and the log lines is replaced by `~/…` before the dialog shows them. That is the
only cleaning: the log lines and the error text are otherwise sent as written. The dialog
shows every line that is sent before you send it, and you can untick the log. A report
carries no doc, session or conversation content, no account details and no installation id.
It is sent only when you press Send, whether or not telemetry is on, and is stored in
Slate's own Supabase project, readable only by the Slate team. What you wrote, the screen,
the error and the version are then copied to a private GitHub issue, so the team can track
the fix; the log lines stay in Supabase. When you turned crash reports on, a crash's type
and stack may be copied to a private GitHub issue in the same way.

**Requests you start yourself.** When you press a button for it, git and `gh` fetch, pull,
push and open pull requests against your own remote. A widget's GitHub action (approve,
request changes, comment or label) runs only after you confirm the card that names the
account. A live artifact can load a script from cdnjs, jsDelivr or unpkg, and that host
sees the address it asks for.

**Connections you set up yourself.** Tasks reads your integrations, and Slate makes some of
those requests itself. The first two kinds start when you connect the tool, and Disconnect
stops them. For an app you connected with a pasted token, Slate sends read requests with that
token to the address you gave it, and follows no link that leaves that address. For a tool
gateway at a web address, and for an app you connected from Slate, it signs in with the token
that server issued to Slate and sends it only to that server. GitHub is read through your own
`gh` sign-in. A toolkit entry already in an agent's own MCP configuration is asked for its
list of tools at its own address, with the key that configuration already holds, when Tasks
syncs and when you let a widget use one of its tools. What these requests
carry is what the other server needs to answer. None of them sends a doc, a session or a
memory of yours.

Aside from your sign-in, the four exceptions, a problem report you send, the requests you
start and the connections described above, Slate makes no outbound network requests with
your workspace data.

## How Long the Cloud Keeps It

| What | How long |
|---|---|
| Usage counts and crash reports | 180 days, then deleted by a daily job in the database |
| Problem reports | 12 months, then deleted by a daily job in the database. The GitHub issue copy is deleted on request to the contact below |
| Your account: profile, plan, Team interest and sign-in logs | Until you delete your account |
| Invitations | Until they are accepted or declined |
| Shared workspace rows you authored | Until you withdraw or erase them, stop sharing, or delete your account |
| Request logs of the update service and the release host | A short time, set by Supabase and GitHub rather than by Slate |

## No Tracking, No Sale of Data

Slate requires an account (see [Your Account](#your-account)). The account holds who you
are and your plan, and no backend receives your docs, sessions, or files unless you have
shared the workspace they are in.

- There is no behavioral analytics, ad tracking, profiling, or background monitoring.
- Your content is never used to train shared, public, or third-party AI models by
  Slate.
- Your data is never sold, rented, or traded.

The filesystem watcher that captures AI sessions (from the conversation files of the AI
tools you connect) runs locally on your machine and writes only into your
local workspace database.

## Third-Party Model Providers

When you use an agent, the underlying CLI communicates with that provider's service.
Those interactions are governed by the provider's own terms and privacy policy, not by
this document:

- The **Claude Code CLI** communicates with Anthropic under Anthropic's terms.
- The **Codex CLI** communicates with OpenAI under OpenAI's terms.
- The **Cursor CLI** communicates with Cursor under Cursor's terms.
- The **Gemini CLI** communicates with Google under Google's terms.
- The **OpenCode CLI** communicates with whichever provider you configured in it, under
  that provider's terms.
- The **GitHub Copilot CLI** communicates with GitHub under GitHub's terms.
- Every other agent you connect communicates with its own vendor, or the provider you
  configured in it, under that party's terms.

You choose which agent to use, and you authenticate those tools yourself. Similarly,
any external MCP server you connect to Slate operates under its own terms; data you
send to a connected tool is handled by whoever runs that tool.

## Service Providers

These companies process data for Slate:

| Provider | What it does for Slate |
|---|---|
| **Supabase**, hosted on AWS in Singapore | Accounts and sign-in, shared workspace rows, opt-in telemetry, problem reports, invitations and the update service |
| **Amazon Web Services** | Supabase's host |
| **GitHub** | Sign-in (if you choose it), the release downloads, and the private issues that problem reports and crashes are copied to |
| **Google** | Sign-in (if you choose it) |

Your own actions also reach third parties that are not Slate's providers: the vendor of each
agent CLI you use, the script hosts a live artifact loads from (cdnjs, jsDelivr, unpkg), the
integrations you connect, and your own git remotes. Each handles that data under its own
terms and privacy policy.

## Your Control, Export, and Deletion

Because each workspace is a single local file, you are in full control of it.

- **Export** — Settings → Workspaces, then the workspace, then Storage offers a one-click copy of
  that workspace's file (`workspace.db` for Personal). Because it
  is just a SQLite file, your data is portable and readable with standard tools.
- **Open the folder** — the same Storage tab can open Slate's data folder directly.
- **Deletion** — deleting a workspace's database file removes that workspace's local data.
  The uninstall command keeps your workspace files unless you pass `--delete-workspace`;
  with it, the folder `~/Library/Application Support/app.slate.workspace/` goes, with
  `machine.db`, the shared workspaces' files and the sign-in files in it. A Personal
  workspace you moved elsewhere is not in that folder and stays. Uninstalling Slate stops all local processing, including the session watcher and
  any scheduled automations. Without that flag it does not touch the telemetry id or consent
  switches described above — those live in `machine.db`, a separate per-machine file, and
  are reset the way that section describes, not by deleting a workspace.
- **Withdrawing shared content** — moving a doc out of a shared workspace removes it from
  that workspace on the next synchronisation.
- **Stop sharing** — switching sharing off for a workspace stops it publishing anything further
  and withdraws what you have already published there: the rows in our database are blanked,
  and every member's copy drops them on their next synchronisation. The workspace and its
  contents remain on your device. If you switch sharing on again, the next synchronisation
  publishes them again.
- **Erasure** — **Erase my work** on a shared workspace deletes every doc, memory and
  activity record you authored there, for every member. Deleting content locally has the same
  effect on the copies: the next synchronisation withdraws from our database anything your device
  no longer holds. It is offered separately from
  *leaving* a workspace, which removes only your own machine's copy and deletes nothing
  upstream.
- **Doc images** — moving a doc out, stopping sharing and **Erase my work** withdraw the doc
  rows, but not yet the images those docs named: they stay in the workspace's private bucket,
  readable only by its members, until removing them is built.

- **Account deletion** — Settings → Account → **Delete my account forever** removes your Slate account
  from our database: your sign-in identity, name, email, plan and Team interest, your
  memberships, the content of the rows you authored in shared workspaces (each row is blanked and marked deleted, keeping only its id, your user id and the time, so teammates' devices delete their copies), invitations you sent or that are
  waiting for you, any account only you were in, and the sign-in audit records that hold your
  email and IP address. It signs you out and leaves everything on your device. While you own an
  account that has other members, Slate asks you to transfer it or remove them first. Some
  copies sit outside our database and are not reached by it: request logs kept by our hosting
  providers, copies already on teammates' devices (which drop your rows on their next
  synchronisation, and the content of a workspace deleted forever, for people who were members
  when it was deleted), anonymous usage counts keyed to this installation (deleted after 180 days),
  and problem reports you chose to send, with their issue copies.

Because every person signs in, our database holds a record of your account even if you
never share anything: your profile (name, email and picture link), your account and plan,
and your Team interest, and Supabase Auth keeps sign-in logs with your IP address.
**Delete my account forever** removes them, along with the shared rows you authored. Your
email address cannot be changed in Slate, because it comes from Google or GitHub. Your workspaces' contents are on our servers only
if you shared a workspace or joined one, and those copies are the rows you authored, removed or
blanked when you erase, withdraw or delete your account.
